label: Story of the Day
claim: Iran says tankers hit mines in Hormuz; the U.S. says the lanes are clear
record_title: Reuters via Arab News, “Iran says ships hit mines in Hormuz, warns vessels to coordinate passage,” Nov. 24, 2026
read: Reuters, in a report carried by Arab News, says Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed that oil tankers hit naval mines, exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz: three on Monday and two more on Wednesday, while transiting an "unauthorised route." U.S. Central Command rejected Monday's claim, saying U.S. forces had cleared all internationally recognized primary shipping routes and that they remain free of mines. Iran's claims of mined, burning tankers are unproven. No ships are named, no images are out, and the regional maritime center calls them unconfirmed. The U.S. denial rests mostly on its own word, but it fits the record. The real message is the threat, aimed at every shipowner in the strait. The Guards named no vessels, owners or crews and released none of the images they promised; the maritime center tracking the strait called the claims unconfirmed, and CENTCOM dismissed similar Guards claims in July and September as false. CENTCOM's denial fits the record (114 U.S.-assisted passages logged Nov. 19-21), but clearing the main lanes doesn't prove no ship hit a mine anywhere, it released no evidence of its own, and it answered Monday's claim, not Wednesday's. The Reuters headline correctly attributes the claim to Iran, but the version we read leaves out the U.S. denial. Graded C across 3 arguments (Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy D; U.S. Central Command B-; Reuters B+). Scorecard: 33% valid, 67% cogent, 50% supported, 80% fallacy-free.
why: Iran's claims of mined, burning tankers are unproven. No ships are named, no images are out, and the regional maritime center calls them unconfirmed. The U.S. denial rests mostly on its own word, but it fits the record. The real message is the threat, aimed at every shipowner in the strait. Key question: If tankers exploded and burned in the strait, why has no ship, owner or crew been named?

headline: CNBC says consumer confidence jumped 11.4 points to 103.3 in November after the midterms, led by Democrats and independents; the Conference Board's release matches
claim: "Consumers grew significantly more optimistic in November in the wake of the midterm elections, with a growing number of Americans now seeing improvement in the labor market and expecting inflation to cool. The Conference Board survey released Tuesday showed improvement across the board, with the headline confidence index jumping to 103.3, up 11.4 points from October" … "Confidence among Democrats and independent voters improved sharply, the Conference Board said, while confidence among Republican respondents fell slightly." — CNBC (Jeff Cox), "Consumer confidence shoots up after Democrats' midterm victories — though inflation worries persist," Nov. 24, 2026
record_title: The Conference Board, "US Consumer Confidence Surged in November" (Consumer Confidence Survey press release, preliminary results), Nov. 24, 2026
why: The Conference Board's Nov. 24 release matches CNBC's numbers: its Consumer Confidence Index rose 11.4 points to 103.3 in November from 91.9 in October, with the Present Situation Index up 13.7 points to 132.8 and the Expectations Index up 9.9 points to 83.6. It also confirms that confidence improved sharply among Democrats and independents while falling slightly among Republicans, that 12-month inflation expectations fell for a second month to 5.7%, and that the jobs 'plentiful' share rose to 30.8% from 26.2% while 'hard to get' fell to 18.4% from 21.4%. The tie to the midterms is the board's own reading: its senior economist said the rally was 'potentially due to lower uncertainty following the midterm elections.'
what_would_change: A revision to the November index when final results come out, or Conference Board data showing the gain came mostly from responses collected before the Nov. 3 election, would change the verdict.
script: CNBC says consumer confidence shot up after the midterm elections, with the Conference Board's index jumping 11.4 points to 103.3, driven by Democrats and independents. The Conference Board's own release matches: the index rose from 91.9 in October to 103.3, confidence rose sharply among Democrats and independents and dipped slightly among Republicans, and inflation expectations eased to 5.7 percent. The board's economist says the rally was potentially due to lower uncertainty after the midterms, and these are preliminary numbers from a survey that started two days before the election. Verdict: matches record.

headline: Fox News says Newsom's blanket commutation of all 548 California death sentences could eventually open a pathway to freedom; his fact sheet confirms the 548, but the sentences become life without parole and many still await state Supreme Court review
claim: "Victim advocates and California prosecutors are pushing back against Gov. Gavin Newsom’s blanket commutation of all 548 death row sentences, arguing the move overrides the will of voters, bypasses individual case reviews and could eventually open a legal pathway to freedom for convicted killers." — Fox News (Louis Casiano), "Gavin Newsom commutes 548 death sentences as victims' advocates slam move," Nov. 24, 2026
record_title: Office of Gov. Gavin Newsom, "FACT SHEET: California Commutations," Nov. 5, 2026; with the governor's Nov. 5 and Nov. 23, 2026 releases
why: Newsom's own fact sheet confirms 548 people are under California death sentences, that the action converts them to life without parole, and that Prop 66 passed 10 years ago, as the advocates say. But the same fact sheet says the commutations do not make anyone eligible for parole and specifically exclude these prisoners from the state's new parole board commutation and resentencing rules, which undercuts the 'legal pathway to freedom' worry the story leaves unanswered. And it isn't yet a completed blanket commutation: for people twice convicted of felonies the state constitution requires California Supreme Court review, Newsom submitted the matter to that court, and his office describes it as a plan and a 'request,' while prosecutors have asked the same court to block it.
what_would_change: A California Supreme Court ruling approving all of the commutations, or a law or rule making commuted prisoners eligible for parole or resentencing, would change the verdict.
script: Fox News says prosecutors and victim advocates are fighting Governor Gavin Newsom's blanket commutation of all 548 California death sentences, warning it could eventually open a pathway to freedom for convicted killers. Newsom's own fact sheet confirms the 548 and that the sentences become life without parole. But it says the action makes no one eligible for parole and bars these prisoners from the state's new resentencing rules. And it isn't final: for people twice convicted of felonies, the state Supreme Court has to review it, and the governor's office calls it a request. Verdict: missing context.

The governor's Nov. 5 release says he 'plans to change' all death sentences, his Nov. 23 release refers to his 'request to commute all death sentences,' and his office's own site calls it a 'proposed action.' The fact sheet also says the action does not release anyone, pardon anyone, change any conviction or erase restitution orders, and that California's last execution was Jan. 17, 2006, consistent with the story. headline: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin calls Kilmar Abrego Garcia a 'human trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator' as he self-deports to Spain; the only criminal case, a human-smuggling indictment, was thrown out in May as vindictive prosecution
claim: "We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Abrego Garcia has self-deported from the United States to Spain. We promised the American people that this human trafficker, wife beater, gang member, and child predator would not remain in our country." — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, DHS statement, Nov. 24, 2026
record_title: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, United States v. Kilmar Armando Abrego Garcia, No. 3:25-cr-00115, Memorandum Opinion (Doc. No. 312), filed May 22, 2026 (Crenshaw, J.)
why: Abrego Garcia's only criminal case, a two-count indictment charging him with transporting undocumented migrants, was dismissed on May 22, 2026, after Judge Waverly Crenshaw found the government failed to rebut a presumption of vindictive prosecution. The Justice Department's appeal is pending, with oral argument set for Feb. 4, 2027. DHS's own release calls him a 'suspected human smuggler' who has been 'accused' of domestic violence and of soliciting images of a minor; we found no court record of a conviction on any of those labels, and he denies the gang allegation.
what_would_change: A Sixth Circuit ruling reinstating the indictment followed by a conviction, or a court judgment finding the domestic-violence, gang or child-exploitation allegations proven, would change the verdict.
outlet: Department of Homeland Security statement, Nov. 24, 2026 (also reported by CBS News and Fox News)
script: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin celebrated Kilmar Abrego Garcia's self-deportation to Spain Tuesday, calling him a human trafficker, wife beater, gang member and child predator. But the only criminal case against him, a federal human-smuggling indictment in Tennessee, was dismissed in May after a judge found the prosecution presumptively vindictive, and the government's appeal won't be argued until February. DHS's own release calls him a suspected smuggler who has been accused of the other conduct. We found no conviction behind any of those labels. Verdict: missing context.
read: Crenshaw's 32-page opinion says DHS reopened a closed investigation of a Nov. 30, 2022, Tennessee traffic stop within days of the Supreme Court's April 2025 order that the government facilitate Abrego's return, and that the Justice Department then indicted him on two counts: conspiring to transport undocumented migrants between 2016 and 2025 and transporting them during the 2022 stop. The court found 'insufficient evidence of actual vindictiveness' but held the government 'failed to rebut the presumption of vindictiveness,' and dismissed both counts. The Sixth Circuit docket (No. 26-5555) shows the government's appeal fully briefed and argument scheduled for Feb. 4, 2027. The DHS release lists the allegations behind Mullin's labels: protective-order petitions filed by his wife in 2020 and 2021, a claim from court filings that he solicited images of a minor, and the government's MS-13 allegation. Those are accusations, not adjudicated findings in any record we located.

headline: Fox News says Florida AG James Uthmeier wants a North Miami Beach doctor's license revoked over at least 149 suspected illegal abortions, each a third-degree felony; the statute matches, but the state's emergency order cites 'more than 50' and only restricts his license
claim: "Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is pushing to strip a North Miami Beach doctor of his medical license over at least 149 suspected illegal abortions, a number he says could rise to 180 as the investigation continues... He said each alleged violation amounts to a third-degree felony." — Fox News (Stepheny Price), Nov. 24, 2026
record_title: Florida Department of Health, In re: Emergency Restriction of the License of Sylvester Reynold Braithwaite, M.D., License No. ME 62140, Case No. 2026-89677, Order of Emergency Restriction of License (Final Order No. DOH261629MQA), signed by State Surgeon General Joseph A. Ladapo, Nov. 24, 2026
why: Florida law backs the felony point: section 390.0111(10)(a) makes willfully performing an abortion in violation of the six-week limit a third-degree felony. But the state's only public record so far, the Department of Health's Nov. 24 emergency order, finds 'over 50' abortions past six weeks between June and September 2026, not 149, and it restricts his license from elective abortions rather than revoking it. The 149 and 180 figures come from 'initial reports' the attorney general cited and that haven't been released, no charges have been filed, and the order says nothing about late-term abortions.
what_would_change: Release of the health department reports behind the 149 figure, an administrative complaint or Board of Medicine action covering that many cases, or criminal charges would change the verdict.
script: Fox News reports Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier wants a North Miami Beach doctor stripped of his license over at least 149 suspected illegal abortions, each one a third-degree felony. The felony part matches Florida law. But the state health department's emergency order, signed Tuesday, cites more than 50 abortions past six weeks, not 149, and it restricts the doctor from elective abortions instead of revoking his license. The higher number comes from reports that haven't been made public, and no charges have been filed. Verdict: missing context.
read: The order, signed by State Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo, finds that 'between June and September 2026, Dr. Braithwaite performed over 50 elective abortion procedures on fetuses that were a gestational age of more than 6 weeks' and 'failed to identify any circumstances' allowing them. It restricts license ME 62140 'to prohibit Dr. Braithwaite from performing any elective pregnancy termination procedures or non-emergency medical abortion procedures' and says a formal discipline case 'will be promptly instituted.' It leaves his other medical practice untouched and can be challenged in a district court of appeal. Florida Statutes section 390.0111(1) bars abortions after six weeks except to save the woman's life or avert serious physical harm, for a fatal fetal abnormality, or up to 15 weeks in documented cases of rape, incest or human trafficking; subsection (10)(a) makes a willful violation a third-degree felony. Fox lists the medical-emergency and rape, incest and trafficking exceptions Uthmeier cited but not the fatal-fetal-abnormality exception. Uthmeier's post on X attributes the 149 figure to 'initial reports from state health officials.'

headline: CNN says Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan asked a federal judge in Kansas to halt his Dec. 3 firing-squad execution, which would be the military's first execution in 65 years; Army records match, though Hasan filed the motion himself with lawyers assisting
claim: "Attorneys for the former US Army major filed a motion Tuesday in US District Court in Kansas to halt the execution while they mount a legal challenge... Hasan's execution — scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood — will be the US Army's first such execution of a soldier since World War II and its first imposition of any death penalty on an armed service member in 65 years." — CNN (Rashard Rose), Nov. 24, 2026
record_title: U.S. Army Public Affairs, "Army Sets Execution Date for Convicted Murderer Nidal Hasan," Oct. 7, 2026
why: The Army's announcement says the acting Army secretary ordered Hasan's execution by firing squad at Fort Hood at 1 p.m. on Dec. 3, 2026, after President Trump approved the death sentence on Oct. 2. The Army's own 2013 report on his sentencing says the last service member executed by the military was Pvt. John A. Bennett, hanged April 13, 1961, so 'first in 65 years' holds; the 'since World War II' line only works as a firing-squad comparison. The District of Kansas docket shows the stay motion filed Tuesday in Hasan v. Sergent and a hearing set, though the motion was filed by Hasan himself, with federal defender and ACLU lawyers helping as standby counsel.
what_would_change: A stay from the Kansas court or the 10th Circuit, or an Army order moving the date, would change the Dec. 3 timeline. Evidence of a U.S. military execution after April 1961 would change the 65-year comparison.
script: CNN reports Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal judge in Kansas to halt his firing-squad execution, set for December 3rd, which CNN says would be the military's first execution in 65 years. Army records match. The Army set the date after President Trump approved the death sentence in October, and its own records say the last military execution was a 1961 hanging. One nuance: Hasan filed the motion himself, with lawyers helping as standby counsel. A hearing is set for Wednesday. Verdict: matches the record.
read: The Army's Oct. 7, 2026, release says Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directed the execution on Oct. 6, that only the president can approve a military death sentence, that Trump did so Oct. 2 after the appeals ran out, and that Army Regulation 190-55 requires a date 60 to 150 days after approval. A court-martial panel convicted Hasan on 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 of attempted premeditated murder and sentenced him to death Aug. 28, 2013; the Supreme Court denied review March 31, 2025. The Army's Sept. 3, 2013, article says the last military execution was Pvt. John A. Bennett's hanging at Fort Leavenworth on April 13, 1961. The District of Kansas docket for Hasan v. Sergent, No. 5:26-cv-03460, shows a stay-of-execution motion filed Nov. 24 and notices of hearing; Law Dork reports Judge Anthony Mattivi set a status conference for 2:30 p.m. CT Wednesday and quotes the filing as pro se, drafted with help from the Fourth Circuit Capital Habeas Unit, with ACLU lawyers as standby counsel.

headline: The Hill says newborn hepatitis B vaccination rates dropped sharply after RFK Jr.-led confusion, to 65.6% in 2026 from about 80%; the study's numbers match, but the decline began in mid-2023 and the study doesn't measure the cause
claim: "Newborn hepatitis B vaccination rates dropped sharply after RFK Jr.-led confusion" … "The rate of infants who received the hepatitis B Virus (HBV) vaccine fell to 65.6 percent in 2026, down from around 80 percent from 2020 to 2022, according to a study published Tuesday in The New England Journal of Medicine." — The Hill (Sarah Davis), Nov. 24, 2026
record_title: Masters, Cartwright et al., "Hepatitis B Birth Dose Vaccination in the United States, January 2018–June 2026," NEJM Evidence Public Health Alerts (in partnership with CIDRAP), DOI 10.1056/EVIDpha2600326, published Nov. 24, 2026
why: The study's numbers match: newborn hepatitis B shots within a day of birth averaged 80.0% from 2020 to 2022 and fell to 65.6% in the first half of 2026, and among babies of mothers who tested positive the rate fell from 97%-98% to 93.9%. But the study says the decline began in mid-2023, about a year and a half before Robert F. Kennedy Jr. became HHS secretary, and it doesn't measure what caused the drop; 'confusion among parents' is the authors' likely explanation, not a finding. The paper ran in NEJM Evidence's Public Health Alerts section, not The New England Journal of Medicine itself.
what_would_change: Data showing newborn hepatitis B vaccination held steady until after Kennedy took office in 2025, or a study that measured parents' reasons and tied the drop to federal guidance changes, would change the verdict.
script: The Hill says newborn hepatitis B vaccination rates dropped sharply after confusion led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., falling to 65.6 percent this year from about 80 percent. The study's numbers match, and the steepest drop came in 2025. But the researchers say the decline started in mid-2023, before Kennedy took office, and the study doesn't measure why parents are skipping the shot. It also ran in NEJM Evidence, not the New England Journal of Medicine itself. Verdict: missing context.
read: The study's numbers match: newborn hepatitis B shots within a day of birth averaged 80.0% from 2020 to 2022 and fell to 65.6% in the first half of 2026, and among babies of mothers who tested positive the rate fell from 97%-98% to 93.9%. But the study says the decline began in mid-2023, about a year and a half before Robert F. Kennedy Jr. became HHS secretary, and it doesn't measure what caused the drop; 'confusion among parents' is the authors' likely explanation, not a finding. The paper ran in NEJM Evidence's Public Health Alerts section, not The New England Journal of Medicine itself. The Hill's line that the drop accelerated after Kennedy took office fits the study's yearly counts: about 77.9% of newborns got the shot in 2023 and 75.4% in 2024, then 69.0% in 2025, the steepest one-year fall in the data. The authors write that the decline 'appeared to accelerate prior to' the vaccine advisory committee's December 2025 vote to drop the universal birth-dose recommendation, and that an earlier study found rates falling from a peak in February 2023. The research used Truveta's electronic health records covering 1,338,961 infants born from January 2018 through June 2026, so it is a large sample, not a national registry count.

headline: Fox News says Biden raised just $1.5 million for his presidential library in 2025, less than 1% of Obama's $232.6 million in 2017; the math holds, but Obama's foundation had been raising money since 2014 and Biden's listed $4 million on its first return
claim: "In 2017, Obama’s first year out of office, the two-term president managed to bring in $232.6 million in donations and contributions to fund the foundation behind his presidential library. By comparison, Biden secured just $1.5 million in 2025 for his presidential library foundation, per tax filings. This is less than 1% of what his former boss raised in the same amount of time after leaving office." — Fox News (Robert Schmad), "Biden's first-year fundraising fails to crack 1% of Obama's library haul as questions swirl over legacy," Nov. 24, 2026
record_title: IRS Form 990 data via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer: Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation (EIN 33-2456598) and The Barack Obama Foundation (EIN 46-4950751); with CBS News, "Biden library nears site decision as fundraising lags," Nov. 16, 2026
why: IRS Form 990 data on ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer show the Obama Foundation took in about $232 million in contributions in 2017, and CBS News, citing a 2025 return it obtained that has not been made public, reported the Biden foundation raised less than $1.5 million last year, so 'less than 1%' holds. But the comparison isn't the same amount of time: the Obama Foundation had been raising money since 2014, while the Biden foundation was incorporated in December 2024, got tax-exempt status in March 2025, and listed $4 million in contributions on its first return, for 2024. The foundation told CBS that 2025 was a 'building and infrastructure year' when it wasn't actively fundraising, and a source said it has since landed gifts including two $5 million donations.
what_would_change: The Biden foundation's public 2025 return showing it raised substantially more than $1.5 million, or records showing the Obama Foundation raised little before Obama left office, would change the verdict.
script: Fox News says Joe Biden raised just 1.5 million dollars for his presidential library in 2025, less than one percent of the 232.6 million Barack Obama raised in 2017. IRS data show the Obama Foundation took in about 232 million that year, and CBS reported Biden's foundation raised under 1.5 million, so the math holds. But it isn't the same timeline. Obama's foundation had been raising money since 2014. Biden's was set up in December 2024, listed 4 million dollars in seed money on its first return, and says it wasn't actively fundraising in 2025. Verdict: missing context.
read: IRS Form 990 data on ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer show the Obama Foundation took in about $232 million in contributions in 2017, and CBS News, citing a 2025 return it obtained that has not been made public, reported the Biden foundation raised less than $1.5 million last year, so 'less than 1%' holds. But the comparison isn't the same amount of time: the Obama Foundation had been raising money since 2014, while the Biden foundation was incorporated in December 2024, got tax-exempt status in March 2025, and listed $4 million in contributions on its first return, for 2024. The foundation told CBS that 2025 was a 'building and infrastructure year' when it wasn't actively fundraising, and a source said it has since landed gifts including two $5 million donations. The IRS data list Obama Foundation contributions of $5.4 million in 2014, $1.9 million in 2015 and $13.2 million in 2016, before Obama left office. For 2017 they show $231,993,748 in contributions and $232,148,718 in total revenue, slightly below the $232.6 million Fox cites, and for 2018 about $163.9 million in contributions, close to Fox's $164.8 million. The Biden foundation's 2024 return shows $4,000,000 in contributions, no expenses and $4 million in net assets. CBS reported the 2025 filing shows about $2.1 million in spending and a deficit of around $600,000, which fits Fox's 'spending $600,000 more than it raised' and the $3.4 million in net assets CBS says the foundation ended 2025 with. headline: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Trump Says He Convinced the Board
claim: “Nvidia (NVDA.O) reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday under pressure from US President Donald Trump, a stunning reversal following his resignation…” — Reuters, Nov. 23, 2026

read: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as president and CEO on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, effective immediately, less than two weeks after he resigned on Nov. 12 following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a businesswoman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. At the company's Nov. 17 earnings call, Chair Harvey Jones had said the board did not intend to reinstate him. President Trump told CNBC he spoke with the board and “convinced them … I made the deal.” Nvidia said that, based on US government input, it was confident “Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk,” and that it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang's candor”; an independent board committee is still investigating whether a foreign intelligence effort targeted Huang, and the company says that probe “will proceed to conclusion.” Nvidia shares closed up 31.5%, adding nearly $1 trillion in market value, according to Reuters. Lawmakers in both parties objected, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb.; Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, asked who in the government weighed in. Huang has agreed to testify at a public Senate hearing on Dec. 3, the Senate Banking Committee said. The company also faces investigations from the SEC, the FBI, California's attorney general and congressional committees, Fortune reports.
why: Fortune's headline says Wall Street “just put a $1 trillion price on Jensen Huang,” but the BBC reports Nvidia's shares remained about 21% below their level a month earlier and that much of the tech rally began in pre-market trading before the announcement, and Reuters says Monday's gains were not enough to erase all losses since Huang's Nov. 12 resignation. The Guardian's headline says Trump “made up to $15m” on Nvidia stock; that figure is an estimate from his financial disclosures, which report holdings in ranges, Reuters' own estimate is “as much as $17 million,” and the Guardian reports Nvidia shares fell 6% in early trading the next day. A White House spokesperson told Reuters the president's portfolio is independently managed.
what_would_change: Updated disclosures showing Trump's actual Nvidia holdings, or the board committee's findings on whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, would change this report.

headline: Russian Warship Sinks at Libya's Benghazi Naval Base After Ukraine Says Its Naval Drones Struck It
claim: “Ukraine has taken its fight against Russia to the shores of North Africa, claiming to have sunk a warship off the coast of Libya in its latest expansion of the war.” — NBC News, Nov. 23, 2026
outlet: NBC News, “Ukraine sinks Russian warship off Libya in latest expansion of the war,” Nov. 23, 2026
record_title: BBC, “Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drones in Libya, Zelensky says,” Nov. 23, 2026
read: An explosion hit a Russian navy ship docked at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya early Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Libya's eastern government said the vessel had stopped to refuel and take on supplies on its way back to Russia, under an existing maritime agreement. On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian-made naval drones sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, commissioned in 2023, and destroyed a Ka-27 helicopter on board; he said the drones also hit the cargo ship MV Angara, which he said Russia used to transport weapons. Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said the drones were launched from a “mother ship” and called both vessels “legitimate military targets.” Satellite imagery from Vantor described by the BBC shows the corvette moored in the port on Saturday and, on Sunday, capsized and sunk with only its forward bow visible. Libya's UN-recognized government in Tripoli and the rival eastern administration both condemned the attack; the eastern government called it “a serious assault on national sovereignty.” The UN Support Mission in Libya called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation,” saying “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov referred questions to Russia's Defense Ministry.
why: NBC News' headline (“Ukraine sinks Russian warship off Libya”) and its X post (“sunk a warship off the coast of Libya”) place the attack offshore; NBC's own report quotes Libya's eastern government saying the vessel was docked at the Benghazi naval base, The Guardian describes Zelenskyy's video showing drones hitting the warship at its berth in the naval base, and Vantor imagery described by the BBC shows it moored in the port. NBC's report does not mention injuries; the BBC reports Libya's health ministry said it received injured people from a commercial ship targeted off the port, and says it is not clear whether that is the same vessel Ukraine claimed.
what_would_change: An official casualty count from Libyan or Russian authorities, or an NBC update reporting injuries or locating the warship outside the port, would change this report.

script:
Coming to you virtually from Benghazi, in eastern Libya. I'm Priya Nair. A Russian warship sank at the naval base here on Sunday, and Ukraine says it did it. Here's the record.
Early Sunday, an explosion hit a Russian navy ship docked at the Benghazi naval base. Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped to refuel and take on supplies on its way back to Russia.
On Monday, President Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian-made naval drones sank the corvette Merkury, commissioned in 2023. He says they also hit a cargo ship, the Angara, which he says carried weapons. Satellite images show the corvette capsized.
Both of Libya's rival governments condemned the attack. The UN mission in Libya called for an independent investigation. The Kremlin referred questions to Russia's Defense Ministry.
How it was told.
One. NBC News' headline and X post say the warship was sunk off Libya, off the coast. The record puts it inside the port, docked at its berth in the Benghazi naval base.
Two. NBC's report doesn't mention anyone hurt. The BBC reports Libya's health ministry received injured people from a commercial ship targeted off the port. It's not clear whether that was the Angara.
Full report at popularalien.com. From Benghazi, Libya, I'm Priya Nair.

script: Fox News reports the DNC's new 2028 debate rules make Democratic candidates denounce super PAC and dark money spending, and refund any spending they approved. The first part checks out. To make the debate stage, candidates must sign a pledge to denounce super PAC and nonprofit ads once a rival reports them. read: The DNC's Fair Campaign Practices Pledge, which candidates must sign to make the debates, matches Fox on the main points: candidates must denounce super PAC and 501(c)(4) ads for or against primary candidates once a rival campaign reports them, and each campaign names one person to report to the DNC. But the refund rule Fox describes doesn't apply to outside groups. The pledge requires refunds only when a campaign requests or approves ads paid for by a state or local Democratic Party committee, and refunds of joint fundraising money. The DNC's 2028 primary page says that 'if the campaign requested or approved the spending, the campaign will need to refund the spending party committee and provide proof of refund,' under the heading 'For party spending.' For super PAC and dark money ads, the only remedy is a one-time denunciation of each group. The DNC's release confirms 12 debates, five in 2027 and seven in 2028, starting in June 2027, and the quote Fox attributes to the DNC about Citizens United appears word for word on its 2028 page. The DNC says it can't ban super PACs or dark money groups, and the pledge doesn't apply to the general election.

script: CNN, reporting on a new Oxfam study of Gaza, says about 85 percent of Gaza's water infrastructure is damaged or destroyed, leaving people with roughly 18 liters of water per person per day. The 85 percent is in the report. The 18 liters isn't a daily supply. The report says that's how much the remaining reservoirs could hold, enough for one day. read: The Oxfam and Conflict and Environment Observatory report does say 'around 85% of Gaza's water infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.' But its 18-liter figure isn't a daily supply: the report says the nine remaining reservoirs hold enough 'to supply Gaza's population with only 18 litres per person for a single day.' The report puts average household water at about 23.5 liters per person per day in April 2026, less than half the World Health Organization's 50-liter minimum. CNN's other figures match the report: Israeli ground operations affected about 78% of Gaza's land area, its spatial analysis found indicators of at least one potential contamination source across more than 99% of the territory, and it cites the UN Environment Programme's estimate of more than 61 million tons of debris. The 99% figure maps contamination risk from satellite and incident data, not measured pollution, and the report says restrictions on testing equipment prevent a full assessment. This check rates CNN's account of the report's numbers, not the report's legal conclusions, which Israel's foreign ministry called 'shameful and scandalous.'

headline: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says American corn and dairy exports 'were up double digits last year' and 'the Chinese are buying 25 million metric tons of soybeans'; USDA data show corn up about 35% and dairy up 15% in 2025, and China's 25 million tons is an annual pledge it is still filling

Countries are coming to the table." — U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, in a TV interview clip posted by the White House's @RapidResponse47 account on X, Nov. 22, 2026
record_title: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service, U.S. Corn Exports in 2025 (with USDA ERS's Ag and Food Statistics: Agricultural Trade, USDA-reported 2025 dairy export totals, the White House's Nov. 2025 China trade fact sheet and ERS's Oil Crops Outlook, Nov. 13, 2026)
why: USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service puts 2025 U.S. corn exports at $18.55 billion, and USDA's Economic Research Service trade tables show about $13.7 billion in 2024, a gain of roughly 35%; USDA's 2025 data put dairy exports at $9.51 billion, up 15%, and ERS confirms both grew while soybean exports fell. The 25 million metric tons is China's pledge, in the White House's November 2025 fact sheet, to buy at least that much U.S. soybeans in each of 2026, 2027 and 2028, and ERS said Nov. 13 that China 'is on the way to completing' it, so it's a commitment still being filled. The data don't show by themselves how much of the gains came from trade deals.
what_would_change: Revised USDA trade data showing 2025 corn or dairy exports grew less than 10% from 2024 would change this, as would USDA export sales data showing China has stopped buying toward, or abandoned, its 25 million metric ton commitment.
script: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says American corn and dairy exports were up double digits last year, and that China is buying 25 million metric tons of soybeans. USDA's numbers back up the first part. Corn exports hit $18.55 billion in 2025, up about 35% from 2024, and dairy exports rose 15% to $9.51 billion. The soybean figure is China's pledge to buy at least 25 million tons a year from 2026 through 2028. USDA says China is on its way to meeting it this year, but hasn't finished. Verdict: matches the record.
read: USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service puts 2025 U.S. corn exports at $18.55 billion on 82.3 million metric tons, and USDA's Economic Research Service calendar-year trade tables show corn at about $13.7 billion in 2024, a gain of roughly 35%; FAS had reported 2024 corn up 6% from 2023. U.S. dairy exports totaled $9.51 billion in 2025, up 15% from 2024 and just under the 2022 record of $9.54 billion, according to USDA calendar-year data reported by the International Dairy Foods Association and Capital Press. ERS's agricultural trade overview says that while soybean exports fell in 2025, corn, tree nuts and dairy exports grew, and that total U.S. farm exports slid to $171 billion as sales to China fell 66%. The 25 million metric tons comes from the White House's November 2025 fact sheet on its China deal, which says China would buy 12 million metric tons in the last two months of 2025 and at least 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans in each of 2026, 2027 and 2028. ERS's Nov. 13, 2026 Oil Crops Outlook says total U.S. soybean export commitments were 30.23 million metric tons as of Oct. 29, versus 17.2 million a year earlier, driven by China, and that 'China is on the way to completing its 25 million metric ton commitment.' So Greer's numbers match USDA's, with the soybean figure a pledge still being filled. USDA's data alone don't show how much of the corn and dairy gains came from trade deals rather than prices, harvests or other demand.

headline: Fox News says Oregon has a 9.9% state income tax rate, a top corporate income tax of 7.6% and a 0.57% corporate activity tax; Oregon's Department of Revenue lists all three, though each is a top rate that kicks in above an income or sales threshold

Cliff Bentz, R-Ore.
record_title: Oregon Department of Revenue, Corporation Excise and Income Tax filing requirements and tax rates (with DOR's Corporate Activity Tax page, its withholding calculator page and 2026 Publication OR-ESTIMATE rate charts)
why: Oregon's Department of Revenue says the corporate excise and income tax is 6.6% on the first $1 million of taxable income and 7.6% above that, and that the corporate activity tax is $250 plus 0.57% of Oregon commercial activity over $1 million. DOR says personal income above the third bracket is taxed at 9.9%, which for 2026 starts at $125,000 of taxable income for single filers and $250,000 for joint filers. All three rates match, but they're top or marginal rates, not what most Oregonians or businesses pay on every dollar, and Bentz's view that they've driven the economy to 'near collapse' is his opinion, not something these records measure.
what_would_change: A Department of Revenue rate schedule or new Oregon law showing a different top personal income tax rate, top corporate rate or corporate activity tax rate in effect now would change this.
script: Fox News, writing about Oregon's lone Republican congressman, Cliff Bentz, says Oregon has a 9.9% state income tax rate, a top corporate income tax of 7.6% and a 0.57% corporate activity tax. Oregon's Department of Revenue lists all three. But they're top rates. The 9.9% applies only to taxable income above $125,000 for single filers, or $250,000 for couples. The 7.6% corporate rate applies above $1 million of profit, and the activity tax applies to sales over $1 million. Verdict: matches the record.
read: Oregon's Department of Revenue says C corporations pay 6.6% on Oregon taxable income of $1 million or less; above $1 million they pay 7.6% on the excess plus $66,000, and excise tax filers pay a minimum tax if it's higher. DOR's Corporate Activity Tax page says the CAT applies to taxable Oregon commercial activity over $1 million and is computed as $250 plus 0.57% of the amount over that threshold, after a 35% subtraction for certain business expenses. DOR's withholding page says Oregon income is taxed at 4.75%, 6.75% and 8.75% in the first three brackets, and all income above the third bracket at 9.9%; its 2026 OR-ESTIMATE rate charts put that top bracket at taxable income over $125,000 for single filers and over $250,000 for joint filers. So the three numbers Fox News cites are Oregon's current top rates. Fox reports Bentz blamed high taxes and progressive regulations for hurting businesses and said voters want to 'reverse this horrible trend.' The article says he won a fourth term with 61% of the vote. Whether the taxes have pushed Oregon's economy toward 'near collapse' is Bentz's opinion, and the tax records don't measure it.

read: The Census Bureau and HUD's Oct. 27, 2026 release on September new residential sales says the median sales price of new houses sold in September 2026 was $400,400, up 3.9% (plus or minus 6.2%) from August's $385,400 and down 3.9% from September 2025's $416,800; the average price was $472,800. NAR's Oct. 13, 2026 Existing-Home Sales report says the September median existing-home price for all housing types was $417,500, up 1.3% from $412,300 a year earlier. So in September new homes were about $17,100 cheaper at the median, while in September 2025 they were about $4,500 more expensive, which supports CNN's point that the trend has reversed recently. NAR's October report, which CNN's story also links, puts the median existing-home price at $416,700. NAR notes that its existing-home sales are based on closings, while Census counts new-home sales at contract signing, so the two series measure slightly different things. CNN's story is mostly about homeowners' complaints of construction defects at new homes, which these price reports don't address.

script: Senator John Kennedy says the president asked for 42 percent more spending on defense, and that only a Republican reconciliation bill can deliver it. The White House budget backs him up. read: The White House's fiscal 2027 budget fact sheet requests $1.5 trillion in total defense resources and calls it 'a $445 billion or 42-percent increase from the 2026 total resource level,' which was about $1 trillion. headline: A White House spokeswoman tells Fox News Biden-era wolf protections helped push the national cattle herd to a 75-year low; USDA's count is the lowest since 1951, but the herd started shrinking in 2019, and USDA points to the cattle cycle and drought
claim: "As a result, the national cattle herd reached a 75-year low, driving up prices for consumers." — White House deputy press secretary Taylor Rogers, after saying the Biden administration's 'radical environmental policies' left ranchers defenseless as 'predators wiped out their livestock,' as quoted by Fox News ("Apex predator at center of farmers vs environmentalists fight as Trump weighs major move: 'Out of control'," Nov. 22, 2026)
record_title: USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service, Cattle report, released Jan. 30, 2026 (with USDA Economic Research Service, Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Outlook, February 2026)
why: The number is right: USDA counted 86.2 million cattle and calves on Jan. 1, 2026, below 2025's count and, based on USDA's historical data, the fewest since 1951. But USDA's Economic Research Service says the herd peaked at 94.7 million in 2019, during Trump's first term, and has shrunk for seven straight years since then. USDA explains the drop with the normal cattle cycle, prices and weather, and its reports don't blame wolves or Biden-era rules.
what_would_change: USDA or other federal data showing that wolf or other predator losses, or specific Biden administration environmental rules, made up a meaningful share of the herd's decline would support the White House's cause-and-effect claim. A new USDA count showing the herd growing again would make the '75-year low' outdated.
script: A White House spokeswoman tells Fox News that Biden-era environmental policies left ranchers defenseless against predators, and as a result the national cattle herd hit a 75-year low. The low is real. USDA counted 86.2 million cattle in January, the fewest since 1951. But USDA's own numbers show the herd peaked in 2019, during Trump's first term, and has shrunk every year since. USDA points to the cattle cycle, prices and drought, not wolves. Verdict: missing context.
read: The number is right: USDA counted 86.2 million cattle and calves on Jan. 1, 2026, below 2025's count and, based on USDA's historical data, the fewest since 1951. But USDA's Economic Research Service says the herd peaked at 94.7 million in 2019, during Trump's first term, and has shrunk for seven straight years since then. USDA explains the drop with the normal cattle cycle, prices and weather, and its reports don't blame wolves or Biden-era rules. The Economic Research Service describes the cattle cycle as herd expansion and contraction driven by cattle prices, feed and other costs, the time it takes to raise cattle and weather, and University of Arkansas extension economists also cite persistent drought. The beef cow herd is the smallest since 1961. The White House statement came in a Fox News story about whether the Interior Department will remove federal protections for gray wolves. Trump's Sept. 4 executive order gives the interior secretary until Dec. 3 to decide whether the gray wolf and Mexican wolf meet recovery criteria. Fox also quoted Defenders of Wildlife saying wolves account for less than 1% of livestock losses. Rancher losses to wolves are real in places like Minnesota, but USDA's herd data doesn't show how much of the national decline, if any, comes from predators.

headline: COP31 Climate Talks in Turkey End Without Their Main Deal After the EU and Others Reject a Text That Omits Fossil Fuels
claim: “UN climate talks ended in collapse on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkey and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.” — Reuters, Nov. 22, 2026
outlet: Reuters, “COP31 climate talks collapse as EU and others reject deal,” Nov. 22, 2026
record_title: UN News, “COP31 ends without climate pact as UN chief warns there is ‘no ambiguity in the science’,” Nov. 22, 2026
read: The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, two days past its Friday deadline, without adopting its overarching political decision. COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, told the closing plenary: “I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted.” UN News calls it the longest UN climate summit on record. The European Union formally objected to the cover decision because it did not mention fossil fuels or a transition away from them; Ireland's Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU, called the omission “unconscionable.” Panama said it could not support the text and the Marshall Islands withheld its support, while Saudi Arabia, speaking for the League of Arab States, defended its references to carbon capture and storage. Reuters reports the text called for tripling adaptation finance without specifying a baseline and included a goal to raise electricity's share of final energy use to 35% by 2035. Commitments agreed at earlier conferences still stand, and the next summit, COP32, is set for Ethiopia in November 2027. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said: “There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”
why: At 12:20 p.m. CT on Sunday, Reuters' X account posted “COP31 climate talks set to collapse without political deal,” about three and a half hours after the same account posted “Countries react as COP31 climate talks collapse” (8:45 a.m. CT) and more than five hours after BBC Breaking reported the talks had failed (7:09 a.m. CT). Reuters' report, as updated Sunday, covers the failed political deal; it does not mention that UN climate chief Simon Stiell told the closing plenary the summit reached an agreement on a just transition, which the BBC describes as progress on a “just transition mechanism” for workers and communities.
what_would_change: A later UNFCCC record showing the just-transition decision was not adopted, or a Reuters update reporting it, would change this report.

script:
Coming to you virtually from Antalya, in Turkey. I'm Marcus Okafor. The UN climate talks here have ended without their main political deal. Here's the record.
On Sunday, two days late, COP31's president, Turkey's Murat Kurum, told the closing session there was no consensus on the text, so the decisions were not adopted. It is the longest UN climate summit on record.
The European Union, Panama and the Marshall Islands refused to back it. The draft never used the words fossil fuels. The EU called that unconscionable. Saudi Arabia defended the text's carbon capture language.
Poorer countries objected that it called for tripling adaptation money with no baseline. Past commitments still stand. Next up is COP32, in Ethiopia.
How it was told.
One. At twelve twenty Central time, Reuters' X account posted that the talks were set to collapse. About three and a half hours earlier, the same account had already posted that they had collapsed.
Two. Reuters' report, as updated Sunday, covers the failed political deal. It doesn't mention what the UN climate chief told delegates: the summit did reach an agreement on a just transition.
Full report at popularalien.com. From Antalya, I'm Marcus Okafor.

script: The Hill reports Democrat Chuck Hubbard still leads Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx by 330 votes after a recount in North Carolina's 5th District. headline: Rep. Lisa McClain says 'it costs nearly FOUR cents to make just one penny' as Trump signs her Common Cents Act; the Mint's latest audited figure is 3.02 cents, and 'nearly four' comes from the year before
claim: "It costs nearly FOUR cents to make just one penny. This legislation will save $85 million per year by permanently ending penny production — it's common sense!" — Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), the Common Cents Act's author, on X on Sept. 29, 2026, as quoted by NBC News (Kyla Guilfoil), "Trump formally ends minting of the penny after nearly 250 years of production," Nov. 20, 2026
record_title: Treasury Office of Inspector General, OIG-26-021, "Audit of the United States Mint's Financial Statements for Fiscal Year 2025" (includes the Mint's 2025 Annual Report and its table "Unit Cost of Producing and Distributing Coins by Denomination"), Feb. 26, 2026
why: The U.S. Mint's audited 2025 Annual Report puts the full cost of making and distributing one penny at 3.02 cents in fiscal 2025, down from 3.69 cents in fiscal 2024, so McClain's 'nearly FOUR cents' matches the older 2024 figure, not the latest one available when she posted in September 2026. The penny still cost about three times its face value, and the report says that was the 20th straight year it cost more than a cent.
what_would_change: A newer Mint cost figure at or near four cents for a later period would make the claim match the record. A Mint or Congressional Budget Office estimate of yearly savings would let the $85 million figure be rated.
script: Rep. Lisa McClain says it costs nearly four cents to make one penny, and President Trump has now signed her bill ending penny production for good. The Mint's own audited numbers tell a slightly different story. Making and shipping a penny cost 3.69 cents in fiscal 2024. In fiscal 2025, the latest year on record, it was 3.02 cents. That's still three times what the coin is worth, but 'nearly four' is last year's number. Verdict: missing context.
read: The U.S. Mint's audited 2025 Annual Report puts the full cost of making and distributing one penny at 3.02 cents in fiscal 2025, down from 3.69 cents in fiscal 2024, so McClain's 'nearly FOUR cents' matches the older 2024 figure, not the latest one available when she posted in September 2026. The penny still cost about three times its face value, and the report says that was the 20th straight year it cost more than a cent. The same report says the Treasury suspended penny production in fiscal 2025 because of the rising cost, and that the Mint shipped 4.8 billion pennies that year for $48.3 million in revenue. The report doesn't give a yearly savings figure, so this check doesn't rate McClain's $85 million estimate; NBC notes the Mint had put the immediate annual savings at $56 million. The White House confirms Trump signed H.R. 10167, the Common Cents Act, on Nov. 20.

headline: CNN says a 9-8 appeals court ruled the 2022 $1.7 trillion spending law unconstitutional because of proxy voting; the Fifth Circuit's opinion matches, but the lower-court ruling CNN dates to 2022 came in 2024
claim: "A federal appeals court ruled Friday that a massive pandemic-era spending law passed during President Joe Biden's administration was unconstitutional because many lawmakers delegated other members to cast votes for them in their absence... in a 9-8 ruling, the majority said proxy votes do not count toward a quorum under a clause in the US Constitution governing congressional meetings, making the law's passage unconstitutional. A US district court judge made the same ruling in 2022." — CNN (Kaanita Iyer), "Biden-era spending law found unconstitutional by federal appeals court," Nov. 21, 2026
record_title: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit (en banc), State of Texas v. Blanche, No. 24-10386, opinion filed Nov. 20, 2026
why: The Fifth Circuit's en banc opinion in Texas v. Blanche, filed Nov. 20, rules 9-8 that the House's COVID-era proxy rule broke the Constitution's Quorum Clause, so the 2022 omnibus wasn't validly passed, and it upholds the injunction blocking enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act against Texas. It cites the 225-201 vote, with one member voting present, and the 226 members who voted by proxy, and it stresses the 'narrow scope' of its judgment, all as CNN reports. But the district court ruling CNN says came in 2022 was issued in 2024, in a case Texas filed in 2023.
what_would_change: A district court ruling in this case dated 2022 would make CNN's account fully match the record. A Supreme Court stay or reversal, or a corrected CNN story, would also change the verdict.
script: CNN reports a federal appeals court ruled nine to eight that the 1.7 trillion dollar spending bill passed in 2022 was unconstitutional because most House members voted by proxy. The Fifth Circuit's opinion backs up the core of that. It says proxies can't count toward a quorum, notes 226 members voted by proxy, and blocks the pregnant-worker law only in Texas. But CNN says a lower court made the same ruling in 2022. That ruling came in 2024. Verdict: missing context.
read: The Fifth Circuit's en banc opinion in Texas v. Blanche, filed Nov. 20, rules 9-8 that the House's COVID-era proxy rule broke the Constitution's Quorum Clause, so the 2022 omnibus wasn't validly passed, and it upholds the injunction blocking enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act against Texas. It cites the 225-201 vote, with one member voting present, and the 226 members who voted by proxy, and it stresses the 'narrow scope' of its judgment, all as CNN reports. But the district court ruling CNN says came in 2022 was issued in 2024, in a case Texas filed in 2023. CNN also says the majority found the government 'did not establish there was an existence of an emergency.' The opinion makes a different point: that nothing in the government's argument 'depends on the existence of an emergency,' so a pandemic can't create a power the Constitution doesn't give. The opinion is by Judge Cory Wilson, joined by eight judges; Judge James Graves wrote the main dissent, joined by six others, and Judge Catharina Haynes dissented separately. The ruling applies only to enforcing the pregnant-worker law against Texas, not to the rest of the spending law.

Coming to you virtually from Guasave, in Mexico's Sinaloa state. I'm Diego Ramirez. One of the FBI's ten most wanted was captured here Friday night. Here's the record.
Mexico's defense ministry says army and National Guard special forces detained Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, here on Friday, working with U.S. intelligence. Two alleged deputies were taken with him.

The three men were flown to Mexico City. He is wanted in Mexico on organized crime charges, faces a U.S. extradition warrant, and carried a five million dollar U.S. reward.

Full report at popularalien.com. From Guasave, Sinaloa, I'm Diego Ramirez.

headline: CBS News says newly released Pentagon UFO files show a contractor planned an underground vault for 'exotic material or tissue'; the 2009 Bigelow report says that, though it describes a plan, not a vault that was built or anything stored in it
claim: "The Pentagon released a new batch of UFO files on Friday, including one report from a government contractor detailing plans for an underground vault to store 'exotic material or tissue' and recovered 'hardware' it hoped to obtain." — CBS News (Stefan Becket), "New UFO files show Pentagon contractor planned underground vault for 'exotic material'," Nov. 20, 2026
record_title: Department of War, PURSUE Release 08, DOW-UAP-D172, "BAASS Ten-Month Report, July 2009" (Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies report to the Defense Intelligence Agency, 538 pages), released Nov. 20, 2026
why: The 538-page July 2009 Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies report, posted by the Department of War in its eighth UFO records release on Nov. 20, says BAASS saw the need for 'a highly secure underground vault' to hold 'recovered hardware and biological samples' from sources 'including Brazil,' since it had no secure place 'to store exotic material or tissue.' It describes plans for a 5,000-square-foot vault in North Las Vegas with '3 foot thick walls,' a thick steel vault door, 15 to 20 feet of earth on top and 'extensively camouflaged' surface structures, matching CBS's account.
what_would_change: Records showing the vault was never planned as described, or that the passage comes from a different document, would contradict CBS. Released records showing the vault was built and actually held recovered material would add to the story, and a document showing the report was officially released before Nov. 20 would undercut the 'first time' framing.
script: CBS News says the Pentagon's newest batch of UFO files includes a contractor's plan for an underground vault to store exotic material or tissue. That checks out. The 2009 report from Bigelow Aerospace's research arm, written for a Defense Intelligence Agency program, lays out a 5,000-square-foot vault in North Las Vegas with three-foot-thick walls, buried under 15 to 20 feet of earth. But it's a plan. Nothing in the files shows it was built or that anything was ever stored in it, and a DIA memo later called the contractor's reports of limited value. Verdict: matches record.
read: The 538-page July 2009 Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies report, posted by the Department of War in its eighth UFO records release on Nov. 20, says BAASS saw the need for 'a highly secure underground vault' to hold 'recovered hardware and biological samples' from sources 'including Brazil,' since it had no secure place 'to store exotic material or tissue.' It describes plans for a 5,000-square-foot vault in North Las Vegas with '3 foot thick walls,' a thick steel vault door, 15 to 20 feet of earth on top and 'extensively camouflaged' surface structures, matching CBS's account. The report itself calls the vault a plan, saying it could be occupied by late 2009 or early 2010 'subject to building permits'; the released records don't show it was ever built, as CBS notes. headline: A Russian cruise missile and two other objects came down in rural southeastern Poland during a massive attack on Ukraine; nobody was hurt, and Warsaw, not NATO, called it intentional
claim: “Russian cruise missile crashes in Poland in violation condemned as intentional” — BBC News (@BBCWorld) on X, Nov. 20, 2026
outlet: BBC News, “Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk,” Nov. 20, 2026
record_title: Polish Ministry of National Defence, Deputy Prime Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz on the violation of Polish airspace, Nov. 20, 2026
read: Poland's defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said three objects violated Polish airspace early Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, during one of Russia's largest air attacks on Ukraine since the full-scale invasion; officials believe two were missiles and one a jet-powered drone. One, identified as a Kh-101 cruise missile, came down in a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in Lubelskie province, about 50 km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border; a suspected second missile fell near Rudnik nad Sanem and the drone near Mołodycz in Podkarpackie province. Nobody was hurt and no damage to infrastructure was reported. Polish F-16s and Swedish Gripens flew through the night and Patriot batteries were activated, but no weapons were fired because, Gen. Ireneusz Nowak said, not all the conditions for engagement were met. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned “grave violations of Polish airspace” and said NATO jets were scrambled. The incursions came as 11 countries held the Koalicja 2026 exercise at Nowa Dęba. Russia has made no comment.
why: The BBC's X post says the violation was “condemned as intentional.” That is Warsaw's assessment: Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident and that it was “no coincidence” the objects landed near the coalition exercise, and the defence minister called it a provocation. NATO's Rutte called the violations “grave” and “clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine,” but did not call them intentional, and Russia has not commented. The BBC's headline says a Russian missile “hits Poland”; the missile came down in a rural area, nobody was hurt, officials said residents were not at risk, and Poland's operational commander said radar data made it difficult to determine the objects' exact types.
what_would_change: Evidence from NATO or Polish investigators that the missiles were deliberately aimed at Polish territory, or confirmed damage or injuries in Poland, would change this report.

script:
Coming to you virtually from Nowy Lipowiec, in southeastern Poland. I'm Priya Nair. A Russian cruise missile came down here on Friday. Here's the record.
Poland's defense minister says two missiles and a jet-powered drone crossed into Polish airspace early Friday, during one of Russia's biggest attacks on Ukraine. Nobody was hurt.
One was identified as a Kh-101 cruise missile. It came down in a rural area here, about fifty kilometers from the Ukrainian border. A suspected second missile fell near Rudnik nad Sanem, and the drone near Molodycz.
Polish and allied jets flew overnight, but no weapons were fired; not all conditions to engage were met. NATO condemned grave violations of Polish airspace. Russia has not commented.
How it was told.
One. The BBC's post says the violation was condemned as intentional. That's Warsaw's view. Prime Minister Tusk said it was no coincidence. NATO called it dangerous, but did not call it intentional.
Two. The BBC's headline says a Russian missile hits Poland. It came down in a rural area. Officials say residents were never at risk, and the military says radar data made it hard to tell exactly what the objects were.
Full report at popularalien.com. From Nowy Lipowiec, Poland, I'm Priya Nair.

headline: The White House says traffic deaths have fallen to the 'second-lowest level in American history' after Trump's truck-driver crackdown; NHTSA says it's the death rate, not the count, that's second-lowest, and its data don't link the 2.5% drop to truckers

record_title: NHTSA, "Early Estimates of Motor Vehicle Traffic Fatalities and Fatality Rate for the First Half (January–June) of 2026," DOT HS 813 875, November 2026
why: NHTSA's early estimate puts first-half 2026 deaths at 16,750, down about 2.5% from 17,175, and says the rate of 1.02 deaths per 100 million miles driven would be the second-lowest first-half rate, behind 1.01 in 2014, so the release's rate claim checks out. But the number of deaths is not the second-lowest ever: NHTSA's own table shows fewer first-half deaths in 2014 (15,035) and 2015 (16,193). The drop also slowed, from 8.1% in the first half of 2025 to 2.5%, with just 0.2% in April through June, and the estimates don't break out truck crashes, so they don't show the decline came from the trucker crackdown.

headline: World Court rules 9-6 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya; it is the first such finding against a state, though the court can't enforce it
claim: “The historic judgement marks the first time the International Court of Justice (ICJ), also known as the World Court, has held a state accountable for genocide in its 80-year history.” — CNN, Nov. 19, 2026
outlet: CNN, “UN top court finds Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against Rohingya minority,” Nov. 19, 2026
record_title: International Court of Justice, The Gambia v. Myanmar (case 178), Judgment of 19 November 2026
read: The International Court of Justice ruled Nov. 19, 2026, in The Gambia v. Myanmar, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State during the 2017 “clearance operations,” and that it also failed to prevent and punish genocide. CNN reports the vote was 9-6; the court's case page lists a joint dissent signed by six judges. Reading the judgment, ICJ President Iwasawa Yuji said “the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy” the Rohingya there. The court rejected Myanmar's argument that it was conducting counterterrorism operations against an insurgent group. It ordered Myanmar to investigate and, if warranted, prosecute those responsible, to allow a safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya, and to pay compensation, with the amount set in a later phase; Myanmar must report back within two years. The judgment is final and binding, but the court has no power to enforce it.
why: CNN says the ruling is the first time the court “has held a state accountable for genocide.” In 2007, in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro, the court found Serbia did not commit genocide but breached the Genocide Convention by failing to prevent the Srebrenica genocide and punish its perpetrators, so the new ruling is the first finding that a state itself committed genocide. CNN's headline also says the court found Myanmar “guilty”; the ICJ decides disputes between states and does not try individuals. It found Myanmar responsible under the Convention and ordered it to investigate and prosecute individuals.
what_would_change: The judgment's own operative clauses showing a different vote, or an earlier ICJ judgment finding that a state itself committed genocide, would change this report.

why: Executive Order 1-74, signed by Whitmire and effective Nov. 6, does bar Houston police from contacting ICE about someone who isn't going to jail, and says suspected immigration status alone is no basis to contact ICE or hold anyone. script: Fox News says Houston Mayor John Whitmire ordered city police to stop notifying ICE when they encounter an illegal immigrant in a nonviolent encounter. read: Executive Order 1-74, signed by Mayor John Whitmire and effective Nov. 6, 2026, says Houston police shall contact ICE about a person only if that person is already going to jail on new charges or other warrants and has a positive National Crime Information Center hit for an ICE administrative warrant; if the person is not otherwise going to jail, officers shall not contact ICE. It also says suspected immigration status alone is not a basis to contact ICE, prolong detention or take someone into custody, and that people must not be held in the field solely for ICE pickup. The order defines a 'jailable offense' as one for which a person can be detained in jail on arrest rather than released on a citation, so the dividing line is custody, not violence: a person booked on a nonviolent jailable charge is still reported, while someone cited and released is not.

read: The Associated Press declared Democrat Mary Peltola the winner of Alaska's U.S. Senate race on Nov. 17, after a count update pushed her share of first-choice votes above 50%, the threshold to win outright and skip ranked choice tabulation. The update put her ahead of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by 12,458 votes out of 287,896 counted, 50.1% to 45.8%, with 99% of the expected vote counted. Earlier, on Nov. 14, the Anchorage Daily News wrote that Peltola was “narrowly crossing the 50% threshold,” but that 50.1% figure left out write-in votes; the state's full results report, which counts them, had her at 49.98% on Nov. 16, according to an Alaska News analysis. what_would_change: State certification of the results, or a concession from Sullivan, would settle the outcome; a final count that dropped Peltola below 50% would send the race to ranked choice tabulation.

headline: Part of the Crimean Bridge collapses after a Ukrainian strike; the road is out of service, and Russia says trains are running on one track
claim: “The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia.” — BBC News, Nov. 17, 2026
outlet: BBC News, “Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine,” Nov. 17, 2026
record_title: Ukraine's General Staff statement on the Kerch Strait Bridge, via Ukrinform, Nov. 17, 2026
read: Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge, which links Russia to occupied Crimea across the Kerch Strait, overnight on Nov. 17. Ukraine's General Staff said an arch and a span of the road section collapsed, that the road section is out of service and no vehicle can cross, and that the railway section is still standing but its arch is damaged. President Volodymyr Zelensky called it “an unprecedented operation” and said it was the seventh stage of an operation lasting several weeks. Russia's Transport Ministry said rail traffic resumed on one track; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would be restored and “will be even better than before,” and Russia's Investigative Committee opened a criminal case on terrorism charges.
why: The BBC wrote that the collapse “has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia,” but the same article reports that the railway section is still standing and that Russia's transport ministry said some rail services resumed. The BBC's headline calls it “Putin's Crimean Bridge”; Russia built the bridge after annexing Crimea in 2014, and the article explains the label, saying the bridge is widely seen as Putin's personal pet project and that he opened it in May 2018.
what_would_change: An official Russian statement or independent imagery showing rail traffic halted again would support “cut off” for rail; engineering assessments of the damaged rail arch would show how long rail service can continue.

script:
Coming to you virtually from the Kerch Strait. I'm Marcus Okafor. Overnight, part of the Crimean Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea fell into the water. Here's the record.
Ukraine's General Staff says an arch and a span of the bridge's road section collapsed. It says the road is out of service and no vehicle can cross. The railway section is still standing, but its arch is damaged.
President Zelensky called it an unprecedented operation, the seventh stage of a weeks-long effort that first destroyed air defense systems, radars and electronic warfare equipment.
Russia's Transport Ministry said rail traffic resumed on one track. The Kremlin said the bridge will be restored, even better than before. Russian investigators opened a terrorism case.
How it was told.
One. The BBC wrote that the collapse cut off Crimea's direct road and rail links with Russia. The same article reports the rail section is still standing, and that some rail services resumed.
Two. The BBC's headline calls it Putin's Crimean Bridge. Russia built it after annexing Crimea in 2014. The article explains the label: it's widely seen as Putin's personal pet project.
Full report at popularalien.com. From the Kerch Strait, I'm Marcus Okafor.

headline: Iran says its drones targeted a US base in Bahrain; Bahrain and the US ambassador say every drone was intercepted
claim: “Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack” — BBC News headline, Nov. 15, 2026

record_title: News of Bahrain, “US Ambassador says all IRGC drones intercepted, no damage or injuries,” Nov. 15, 2026
read: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said six drones targeted a U.S. air defense radar at Bahrain's Al-Riffa helicopter base on Nov. 15, its second claimed attack on Bahrain in three days. Bahrain's military said its air defenses intercepted the attacks before they could achieve their objectives, and U.S. Ambassador Stephanie Hallett said all drones were intercepted with no damage or injuries, calling the IRGC's claims false. The BBC headline states the target as fact although it comes only from the IRGC's statement; on Friday, U.S. Central Command said it shot down two Iranian drones with no injuries or damage.
why: The attack attempt is confirmed by Bahrain, but the target and any hit rest only on the IRGC's own statement. Bahrain and the U.S. ambassador say every drone was intercepted, with no damage or injuries.
what_would_change: Imagery or an official U.S. or Bahraini account showing damage at Al-Riffa would support Iran's claim of a hit; a CENTCOM statement on the Nov. 15 attack would add a U.S. military account to the ambassador's.

France 24 (AFP), “Iran claims drone attack on US military airbase in Bahrain,” Nov. 15, 2026

script:
Coming to you virtually from Manama, Bahrain. I'm Lena Sato. Sirens sounded here before dawn on Sunday, and Iran says it attacked a U.S. base. Here's the record.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said six of its drones targeted a U.S. air defense radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base. The statement, posted by Iran's state broadcaster, added that the Strait of Hormuz is closed.
Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued an alert at about four thirty a.m. and told residents to proceed to the nearest safe location. Bahrain's military said its air defenses intercepted the attacks before they could achieve their objectives.
The U.S. ambassador to Bahrain, Stephanie Hallett, said all the drones were intercepted, with no damage or injuries, and called the Guard's claims false. On Friday, U.S. Central Command said it shot down two Iranian drones, with no injuries or damage.
How it was told.
One. The BBC's headline says Iran targets a U.S. military base. That target comes only from the Revolutionary Guard's own statement, and Bahrain says the attacks were intercepted.
Two. Al Jazeera wrote that the Guard said it struck the radar. Its explainer noted the U.S. military had not yet commented, but left out the U.S. ambassador's statement that the claims were false.
Full explainer at popularalien.com. From Manama, I'm Lena Sato.

why: The Atlanta Fed's Wage Growth Tracker, the record this check used, shows the opposite of the claim: in its latest 12-month average (September 2026, updated Oct. 8), median wage growth was 3.4% for the lowest-paid quarter of workers and 3.8% for the highest-paid quarter. headline: CNN says a 2022 law bans Russian diesel imports unless the president certifies Russia has ended its war in Ukraine; the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act sets out those conditions
claim: "The Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022 bans Russian-origin energy products, including diesel fuel, from being imported into the US ‘unless — following a period for consultation with Congress — the President certifies to Congress that Russia has ceased military hostilities in Ukraine, that Russia poses no immediate military threat to NATO members, and that Russia recognizes the right of Ukrainians to choose their government,’ the lawmakers warned." — CNN (Jennifer Hansler and Avery Schmitz), "Russian diesel under Trump deal struggles to reach US market amid legal fears and criticism," Nov. 15, 2026
record_title: Public Law 117-109, Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act (H.R. 6968), 136 Stat. 1154, approved April 8, 2022 (U.S. Government Publishing Office)
why: Public Law 117-109 bans all Russian products in chapter 27 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, the chapter covering mineral fuels and oils, including diesel, and lets the president lift the ban only after consulting four congressional committees at least 45 days ahead and certifying that Russia has agreed to withdraw its forces and end hostilities on terms Ukraine accepts, poses no immediate threat to any NATO member, and recognizes Ukrainians' right to choose their government. CNN's summary of the lawmakers' warning tracks those conditions; the law adds that a termination takes effect only after 90 days, and Congress can block it with a joint resolution of disapproval. The law also says the ban applies "in a manner consistent with" actions taken under Executive Order 14066, wording relevant to the Treasury waiver CNN says lawmakers are disputing.
what_would_change: A later statute repealing or amending the 2022 act, a presidential certification under its Section 3, or a court ruling that the Treasury waiver lawfully permits imports would change how this claim stands.
script: CNN reports that lawmakers warned a 2022 law bans Russian diesel imports unless the president certifies Russia has ended its war in Ukraine, poses no threat to NATO, and respects Ukraine's right to choose its government. The Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act says exactly that, after consulting Congress, and adds a 90-day wait that Congress can block. It also ties the ban to the executive order Treasury's waiver relies on. Verdict: matches the record.
